title: Why Airplane Windows Are Round (It Cost 56 Lives)

thumbnail.plane: side view of a modern white passenger jet airliner flying above the clouds at golden hour, the full aircraft from nose to tail, a long row of small rounded cabin windows clearly visible along the fuselage, dramatic sky
thumbnail.zoom: extreme close-up of a single airplane cabin window seen from outside on a white fuselage, the window has smooth rounded corners, rivets around the frame, sky reflected in the glass

shots.vo: In 1954, two of the most advanced airliners in the world fell out of a clear sky.
shots.prompt: a 1950s silver jet airliner breaking apart high above a calm blue Mediterranean sea, debris trailing, clear daylight sky, seen from far away

shots.vo: Fifty-six people died.
shots.prompt: an empty sunlit 1950s airliner cabin with rows of seats, quiet and still, dust in the light

shots.vo: And the reason is right next to you, every time you fly.
shots.prompt: a passenger's view of a modern airplane cabin window with rounded corners, the wing visible outside above white clouds

shots.vo: So why are airplane windows round?
shots.prompt: close-up of a rounded airplane window in a dark cabin, a single beam of light coming through it

shots.vo: Look out of any airliner today and the window is a soft oval. No sharp corners. Ever.
shots.prompt: a row of oval airplane cabin windows on the inside wall of a modern airliner, soft shapes, warm reading lights

shots.vo: Most of us assume it is about looks. Or the view. Or that curved glass is just easier to make.
shots.prompt: a traveler with headphones looking out of a rounded airplane window at clouds, silhouette, back view, no face visible

shots.vo: It is none of those things. The real answer begins with the first jet airliner the world ever built.
shots.prompt: a polished silver 1950s jet airliner standing on an airfield at dawn, four engines buried in the wings, long row of large squarish cabin windows

shots.vo: May 1952. The de Havilland Comet enters service. It is the first jet airliner to carry paying passengers.
shots.prompt: a 1950s silver de Havilland Comet style jet airliner taking off from a runway, crowds watching behind a fence, black and white newsreel mood painted in color

shots.vo: It flies almost twice as high as the propeller planes of its day, above the weather, smooth and quiet.
shots.prompt: a sleek 1950s jet airliner flying very high above a sea of clouds, a propeller airliner far below it, deep blue upper sky

shots.vo: To keep people alive that high, the cabin is pressurised. Air is pumped in until the fuselage swells like a balloon.
shots.prompt: cutaway illustration of a 1950s airliner fuselage with air flowing inside, glowing arrows pushing outward on the metal skin, technical painting

shots.vo: And along its sides runs a row of large, almost square windows. Passengers love them.
shots.prompt: inside a 1950s jet airliner cabin, large nearly square windows with slightly rounded small corners, passengers in 1950s clothing looking out, no faces in focus

shots.vo: Then, on the tenth of January 1954, BOAC Flight 781 climbs out of Rome, bound for London.
shots.prompt: a silver 1950s jet airliner climbing over the coast of Italy in morning light, Rome far below

shots.vo: Near the island of Elba, it breaks apart in the air. All thirty-five people on board are lost.
shots.prompt: the island of Elba seen from high above, a calm sea, a faint trail of smoke in the sky, somber mood

shots.vo: Fishermen watch pieces of the aircraft fall into the sea.
shots.prompt: 1950s Italian fishing boats on a calm sea, fishermen looking up at debris falling from the sky, painted from behind

shots.vo: The Comets are grounded. Engineers suspect fire, or an engine failure, and make changes. Within weeks, the jets are flying again.
shots.prompt: 1950s engineers in overalls inspecting the jet engine bay of a silver airliner in a hangar, work lights, tools

shots.vo: Then, on the eighth of April, South African Airways Flight 201 leaves Rome for Cairo.
shots.prompt: a silver 1950s jet airliner in South African Airways colors climbing into an evening sky over Italy

shots.vo: Near Naples, it vanishes from the sky. Twenty-one more people are gone.
shots.prompt: the Bay of Naples at dusk with Mount Vesuvius, an empty darkening sky, haunting stillness

shots.vo: Two identical aircraft. Two clear days. No storm, no bomb, no pilot error anyone can find.
shots.prompt: two identical silver jet airliners side by side in a dark hangar, a single overhead light, ominous

shots.vo: The world's most modern airliner is taken out of service. And Britain launches one of the largest air crash investigations ever attempted.
shots.prompt: a large 1950s investigation room with long tables of twisted aluminium wreckage, investigators in suits and lab coats examining it, seen from above

shots.vo: The Royal Navy searches the seabed off Elba and lifts piece after piece of the first Comet from the water.
shots.prompt: a 1950s Royal Navy salvage ship on the sea off Elba lifting a twisted piece of aircraft fuselage out of the water with a crane

shots.vo: At Farnborough, the fragments are laid out and rebuilt, like a giant puzzle.
shots.prompt: inside a huge hangar, the wreckage of a silver airliner fuselage reassembled on a wooden frame, pieces missing, engineers measuring

shots.vo: But the wreckage cannot show what happened in the air. So the investigators try something no one has done before.
shots.prompt: a complete silver 1950s jet airliner fuselage being lowered into a giant water tank in a hangar, wings sticking out through the sides

shots.vo: They put a whole Comet into a giant tank of water, and they fly it, over and over, without it ever leaving the ground.
shots.prompt: a 1950s airliner fuselage submerged in a massive water tank, pipes and pumps around it, engineers watching gauges

shots.vo: Water is pumped into the cabin to push it out, as if it were at cruising height. Then released. Then again. Each cycle is one flight.
shots.prompt: close-up of 1950s pressure gauges and valves on a test rig, needles rising, water pipes, dramatic light

shots.vo: After about three thousand flights' worth of cycles, the fuselage splits open.
shots.prompt: a split in the aluminium skin of an airliner fuselage underwater, a long jagged crack, bubbles escaping

shots.vo: The crack starts at a corner. The sharp corner of a squarish opening in the skin.
shots.prompt: extreme close-up of the sharp corner of a square window cutout in aluminium aircraft skin, a hairline crack running from the corner through a rivet hole

shots.vo: Here is why. When the cabin swells, the metal around every opening is pulled tight. Around a smooth curve, that stress flows evenly.
But at a sharp corner, it piles up into one tiny point. There, the metal is pulled far harder than anywhere else.
Every flight stretches that point a little. Not enough to break. Just enough to tire it.
shots.prompt: macro view of metal grain with tiny fatigue cracks forming at a sharp corner, scientific painting

shots.vo: Engineers call it metal fatigue. Tiny cracks grow, flight after flight, invisible, until one day the skin can no longer hold.
shots.prompt: a hairline crack spreading across polished aircraft aluminium, light glinting off the edges, close-up

shots.vo: And when a pressurised cabin fails at thirty thousand feet, it does not leak. It bursts.
shots.prompt: high above the clouds, an airliner fuselage bursting open, a cloud of vapour, seen from a distance, sober and not graphic

shots.vo: Pieces recovered from the sea told the same story. On the Elba Comet, the break had started at the corner of a small square opening in the roof.
shots.prompt: a recovered piece of airliner roof skin with a small square opening, its corner torn, laid on a workbench under a lamp

shots.vo: The lesson changed aviation. When the Comet returned in a new version, its windows were oval.
shots.prompt: a 1950s silver jet airliner with oval windows flying above clouds in bright sunlight, a hopeful mood

shots.vo: Today every airliner on Earth has windows with rounded corners, so the stress flows around them instead of gathering in one place.
Your cabin still swells a little on every flight, and shrinks again when you land. Thousands of times over its life.
shots.prompt: a modern passenger jet at night at an airport gate, cabin lights glowing through its row of rounded windows

shots.vo: And it survives, because the shapes in its skin were designed by what happened in 1954.
shots.prompt: close-up of the rounded corner of a modern airplane window frame from inside, soft light, the engine of the wing outside

shots.vo: So the next time you lean against that little oval window, remember the fifty-six people who taught us its shape.
shots.prompt: a child's hand touching a rounded airplane window, sunset clouds outside, warm amber light

shots.vo: And that is the hidden why.
shots.prompt: a single rounded airplane window glowing in a dark cabin, centered, quiet
